vignette:
Alex presents as a man holding himself together with sheer force of will. In my office, he sits perfectly still, his hands resting on his knees, a stark contrast to the tremor of anxiety I can see in his jaw. He speaks about his life in the clipped, precise manner of a tax consultant, as if he can organize the chaos of his past into neat columns on a spreadsheet. But the numbers, he admits, never quite add up.

Twelve years ago, he was Sergeant Miller, leading a four-vehicle convoy outside of Kandahar. He remembers the heat, the way the sun baked the dust until it seemed to shimmer. He describes the moment not as a memory but as a scene he is forced to re-watch, night after night. It wasn't the initial blast that stayed with him the most. It was the silence that followed—a thick, ringing void where the familiar rumble of the MRAP’s engine should have been. Then came the screaming. He was thrown from the turret, landing hard in a ditch. His own pain was a distant signal. He scrambled back to the road, his ears filled with a high, thin whine, and saw the wreckage of the lead vehicle. That’s where his friend, Corporal Davis, had been. The image of the twisted metal, the smell of diesel and something else, something acrid and sweet, is a permanent fixture in his mind.

He came home a year later with a Purple Heart and a limp that has since faded. He met Sarah, fell in love with her easy laugh, and threw himself into building a new life. He went to college on the GI Bill, found he had a knack for the rigid logic of tax law, and built a successful career. From the outside, he had made the transition seamlessly. He was a husband, a homeowner, a respected professional.

But the war came home with him, an uninvited guest in his quiet suburban life. He finds himself scanning rooftops on his drive to work, his body tensing at the sight of a discarded box on the side of the road. A car backfiring can send a jolt of pure, chemical panic through him, leaving him trembling and slick with sweat. He hasn't had a full night's sleep in years. Most nights, he wakes up gasping, the phantom smell of burning diesel in his nostrils, the image of the wreckage seared onto the back of his eyelids.

His work is his only refuge. The intricate maze of the tax code demands his complete attention, a cognitive fortress that keeps the memories at bay. For eight to ten hours a day, he can be Alex the consultant, the man who finds solutions in a world of rules and regulations. But the moment he leaves the office, the walls crumble.

The hypervigilance has bled into every corner of his life. He can’t go to the movies because the sudden, loud noises in the dark are unbearable. He avoids Fourth of July parties and crowded restaurants, always needing to sit with his back to a wall, his eyes tracking every entrance and exit.

The hardest part for him, he says, is the feeling of being a ghost in his own family. He sees his wife, Sarah, trying to reach him, her face a mixture of love and deep, weary sadness. She’ll touch his arm, and he’ll flinch. She’ll tell him a funny story from her day, and he’ll watch her mouth move but feel nothing, a profound numbness where joy or love should be. He knows he is irritable, that his anger flares over the smallest things—a misplaced set of keys, a dish dropped in the kitchen. He sees the hurt in her eyes afterward and is consumed by a guilt so heavy it feels like a physical weight on his chest. He feels fundamentally broken, a different person from the man she married, and he doesn't know how to find his way back.
